article.title: ‘Traitors in every family’: Hungary to unmask communist-era informants and confront past
article.full_text: Hungary’s new government will on Wednesday reveal the names of tens of thousands of state informants from the communist era in an attempt to confront the past and rebuild public trust. From 1945 to 1989, Hungary’s communist state-security services relied on an extensive network of informants to monitor society and suppress dissent. Some were blackmailed or coerced into reporting on neighbours, friends, colleagues and even family members; others were recruited through promises of various advantages. For decades, the extent of this network was hidden from public view. The “agent files”, held in the basement of the Historical Archives of the State Security services, remained largely inaccessible to the public, despite repeated calls and partial leaks. During his campaign leading up to Hungary’s April parliamentary elections, Péter Magyar promised to make the state-security files public, a promise he seems intent on fulfilling now he is in power. In September, his government passed a law paving the way for the files to be made public, a move more than two-thirds of the country supported according to polls. The release was initially scheduled for the anniversary of the 1956 anti-Soviet revolution but was pushed back to 4 November. “A democratic society has the right to know its past,” Zoltán Tarr, the minister of social relations and culture, wrote on Facebook. Previously, access to the reports on informants was restricted to researchers and relatives of victims. With the new, searchable online database, Hungary’s former state-service will become the most transparent in the former eastern bloc, researchers say. “We are opening wide a door that was left ajar,” said István Papp, a historian and head of the academic department of the archives. “As a historian, I agree with the release of the files. But on a personal level, I feel for those who will face their family’s history for the first time,” Papp said. Of the 50,000 to 60,000 people whose names appear in the files, historians estimate 10% are alive today. For three decades, the former eastern bloc has been divided on how to publish agent files, and when. In East Germany, the Bundestag opened state security Stasi files in 1992. In the Czech Republic, they became open to the public in 2003. Most recently, Latvia published files on informants in 2018. Miklós Kiss, a survivor of a Hungarian forced labour camp and president of an association for victims, would have preferred if Hungary had followed Germany’s example and released the files earlier. “If that would have happened, everything would be done and dusted by now. “People will learn that there were traitors in every family, in every neighbourhood and street,” he added. “But what are we supposed to do with that now?” Placed side by side, the documents would stretch for three miles, enough to trace the perimeter of London’s Hyde Park. Even so, the collection is small compared with that of the Polish or Romanian secret services, Papp said. In Hungary, many files were destroyed during the 1956 anti-Soviet uprising; others disappeared during the transition of 1989, a gradual, largely peaceful process that gave the authorities time to get rid of incriminating material. Many of the records will be incomplete, as the agent’s motivation, or extent of reporting, will remain unknown. Of the 60,000 people mentioned in the files, the archives include detailed files, background checks and statements for only 9,000 people. These will be released in February, after personal information, including details of health, addictions and sexuality, as well as information about victims, has been redacted in accordance with privacy laws. Alexander Faludy, a freelance journalist and Anglican priest, read the files on his family almost two decades ago. His grandfather, György Faludy, spent more than three years in a Hungarian labour camp on fabricated accusations, and later while in exile wrote his book, My Happy Days in Hell. Great Britain’s worst-ever bluetongue season ‘a major animal welfare crisis’
article.full_text: The worst bluetongue season on record has been a major animal welfare crisis in Great Britain, MPs have been told, putting farmers under “severe emotional stress”. Bluetongue, a viral disease that affects sheep, cattle and goats, can cause fever, lesions, stillbirths and death. The tongue may go blue and protrude from the mouth. The virus, which originated in Africa and is transmitted via biting midges, has spread to Europe over the past two decades, a development the World Organisation for Animal Health links to climate breakdown. The strain of bluetongue currently affecting livestock, serotype 3 (BTV-3), was first found in England in 2023. The 2025-26 season has been the worst on record. There have been 3,472 cases recorded in England, Scotland and Wales since July, more than five times the past three seasons combined. Catherine McLaughlin, the chief animal health and welfare adviser at the National Farmers Union, told MPs that this year’s outbreak had placed farmers across the country “under severe emotional pressure and stress”. “Farmers have faced animal deaths, severe disease, reproductive losses, milk and growth losses, extra labour, veterinary costs, disruption to breeding and sales,” she said. “The emotional turmoil this has placed on farms has been really stark and quite distressing to see.” The effect of the virus on animal fertility was likely to have long-lasting effects for farms, she said. “We may well be looking at a lot of farms with very low, low numbers of lamb in the spring, which has a massive financial impact on those businesses.” Dr Gwen Rees, the president of the British Veterinary Association, said because there was no direct treatment for bluetongue, there was little that vets could do. “You can support those animals and hope they get through it, but that’s a very difficult position to be in for a vet and for a farmer,” she said. “It was a major animal welfare crisis.” The cost of vaccination and uncertainty about the risk of infection had deterred some farmers from immunising their animals before the outbreak took hold, Rees told MPs. “Farmers and vets are always balancing risk and benefit and it’s very difficult sometimes to invest in a just-in-case when your margins are extremely tight. The vaccine isn’t a cheap vaccine.” The worst-hit areas have been in the south-west. Devon has recorded 1,291 cases, Somerset 373 and Cornwall 352. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs defines a case as a premises where at least one animal with bluetongue is present, so the total number of animals affected is likely to be higher than the number of reported cases.
